Right: the tree it builds, with nodes numbered depth first: the root 1, outlined in the accent color, the leaf 2 in teal and node 3 with its leaves 4 and 5 in violet." width="100%"} This is the decoder for `to_nested_tuple()`: the empty tuple `()` is a single node, and a tuple of `k` codes is a root joined to the roots of the `k` trees they describe. It is a quick way to write down a tree by its shape, such as `((), ((), ()))` for a root with a leaf child and a child that has two leaves. The nodes are labeled `"1"` to `"n"` (with IDs `1` to `n`), and the root is always node `"1"`. By default the numbering follows a depth-first walk that finishes each subtree before starting the next; with `sensible_relabeling=True` it goes level by level instead, so the root's children come next, then their children, and so on. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [sequence]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [tuple]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The nested tuple code. Lists are accepted in place of tuples. [sensible_relabeling]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, number the nodes in breadth-first order from the root. If `False` (the default), number them in depth-first order. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected, unweighted tree with one node per tuple in the code. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the code holds something other than tuples or lists. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The decoder walks the code with an explicit stack (or a queue, for breadth-first labels), giving each tuple the next node number and an edge to its parent's node, in $O(n)$ time without recursion. NetworkX numbers the nodes from `0`, building the tree with repeated `join_trees()` calls whose default numbering is not a simple walk order; its docs only promise a tree of the same shape, which this also gives. With `sensible_relabeling=True` both visit children in tuple order, so the trees match NetworkX's exactly, with every label shifted up by one. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A root with a leaf and a two-leaf child: ::: {#8a22009e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec tree = ec.Graph.from_nested_tuple(((), ((), ()))) tree.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['1--2', '1--3', '3--4', '3--5'] ``` ::: ::: Breadth-first labels number the levels in turn: the root's children are `"2"` and `"3"`, and the grandchildren `"4"` and `"5"`: ::: {#a91e0d11 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph.from_nested_tuple(((), ((), ())), sensible_relabeling=True).get_edges_str_repr( use_labels=True ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['1--2', '1--3', '3--4', '3--5'] ``` ::: ::: Decoding and re-encoding from the root gives the code back: ::: {#4e786bc1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} code = (((), ()), (), ((),)) ec.Graph.from_nested_tuple(code).to_nested_tuple("1") == code ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: :::
